'''Ernest Armstrong McCulloch''' {{Post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|OOnt|FRS|FRSC}}<ref name=rsbm>{{cite journal |last1=Mak |first1=Tak Wah  |authorlink1=Tak Wah Mak |title=Ernest Armstrong McCulloch. 21 April 1926 — 20 January 2011 |journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] |year=2017 |volume=64 |pages=317–339 |issn=0080-4606 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2017.0019|doi-access=free }}<!-- NOTE: the DOB reported by the Royal Society conflicts with that reported by other sources. --></ref> (27 April 1926<ref name="nyt-2011feb01">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/02/01/health/research/01mcculloch.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |first=Lawrence K. |last=Altman |title=Ernest McCulloch, 84, Crucial Figure in Stem Cell Research |date=1 February 2011}}</ref> – 20 January 2011)<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.uhnres.utoronto.ca/news/php/readarticle.php?id=31327 |title=Dr. Ernest McCulloch (1926–2011) <nowiki>[</nowiki>Death Notice<nowiki>]</nowiki> |publisher=[[University Health Network]] |date=21 January 2011}}</ref> was a [[University of Toronto]] [[cellular biology|cellular biologist]], best known for demonstrating – in a [[Till & McCulloch|partnership]] with  [[James Till]] – the existence of [[stem cell]]s.<ref name="nyt-2011feb01" />

==Biography== 
McCulloch was born in [[Toronto]], Ontario, Canada on 27 April 1926,<ref name="nyt-2011feb01" /><ref name="utlibrary">{{cite web |url=https://discoverarchives.library.utoronto.ca/index.php/mcculloch-ernest-armstrong |title=McCulloch, Ernest Armstrong |work=[[University of Toronto]]}}</ref> and was educated at [[Upper Canada College]] and the [[University of Toronto]].<ref name="star-2009oct11">{{cite news |url=https://www.thestar.com/comment/article/708640 |title=They discovered stem cells ... |newspaper=[[Toronto Star]]|date=11 October 2009 |first=Megan |last=Ogilvie}}</ref>

Ernest McCulloch received his MD in 1948 from the University of Toronto. Upon graduation, he began his education in research at the [[Lister Institute]] in [[London]], England.

In 1957 he joined the newly formed [[Ontario Cancer Institute]], where the majority of his research focused on normal blood-formation and [[Leukemia|leukaemia]]. Together with his colleague, Dr. J.E. Till, McCulloch created the first quantitative, clonal method to identify stem cells and used this technique for pioneering studies on stem cells. His experience in [[hematology]], when combined with Till's experience in [[biophysics]], yielded a novel and productive combination of skills and interests.

In the early 1960s, McCulloch, and Till started a series of experiments that involved injecting [[bone marrow]] cells into irradiated mice.  Visible nodules were observed in the spleens of the mice, in proportion to the number of bone marrow cells injected.  Till and McCulloch called the nodules 'spleen colonies', and speculated that each nodule arose from a single marrow cell: perhaps a stem cell.

In later work, [[Till & McCulloch]] were joined by graduate student Andy Becker, and demonstrated that each nodule did indeed arise from a single cell. They published their results in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' in 1963. In the same year, in collaboration with [[Louis Siminovitch|Lou Siminovitch]], a trailblazing Canadian molecular biologist, they obtained evidence that these cells were capable of self-renewal, a crucial aspect of the functional definition of stem cells that they had formulated.{{citation needed|date=November 2016}}

McCulloch's later research was on cellular and molecular mechanisms affecting the growth of malignant blast stem cells obtained from the blood of patients with [[Acute myeloid leukemia|Acute Myeloblastic Leukemia]].

In 1969, McCulloch won the [[Canada Gairdner International Award]] with [[James Till|James E. Till]] in recognition of their development of the spleen colony technique for measuring the capacity of primitive normal and neoplastic cells to multiply and differentiate in the body.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=All Gairdner Awards Laureates |url=https://gairdner.org/winners/index-of-winners/ |access-date=2022-10-06 |website=Gairdner Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> This technique has been applied by them and their colleagues, and by many others, to gain important knowledge of the normal formation of blood cells, the behavior of leukemic cells and methods of treating leukemia, and other aspects of cell biology.<ref name=":0" />

In 1974, McCulloch became a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]].  In 1988, he became an Officer of the [[Order of Canada]] and was made a member of the [[Order of Ontario]] in 2006.  In 1999, he was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].<ref name="rsbm" />  In 2004, McCulloch was inducted into the [[Canadian Medical Hall of Fame]].  He holds the distinguished title of University Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Toronto]].

In 2005, he and James Till were awarded the [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]].
